entities.summary:
Henry Chichele, a towering ecclesiastical and political figure of late medieval England, served as Archbishop of Canterbury from 1414 until his death on April 21, 1443. His career spanned the reigns of Henry V and Henry VI, periods marked by the Hundred Years' War, significant Lollard dissent, and the burgeoning intellectual life of Oxford. As Primate of All England and a trusted royal counselor, Chichele played a pivotal role in shaping both church policy and national diplomacy, advocating for English interests abroad and consolidating the orthodox faith at home. His enduring legacy is inextricably linked to the foundation of All Souls College, Oxford, a unique institution dedicated to prayer for the fallen of the French wars and the advancement of legal and theological scholarship.

Chichele's ascent to the archbishopric followed a distinguished career in royal service, including diplomatic missions to France and Pope Gregory XII. During his primacy, he actively supported Henry V's campaigns in France, notably delivering a speech in the 1414 Leicester Parliament that encouraged renewed war, partly to divert attention from Lollard demands for church reform. He presided over a period of intense suppression of Lollardy, including the burning of John Oldcastle in 1417, and worked to maintain ecclesiastical discipline through numerous provincial councils. His administrative acumen was also evident in his efforts to reform monastic houses and address clerical abuses, though he faced challenges from papal encroachments on English church autonomy, particularly concerning appointments and financial levies.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Henry Chichele's long primacy as Archbishop of Canterbury (1414-1443) significantly shaped English religious and political life, including his vigorous suppression of Lollardy and his pivotal role in supporting the Hundred Years' War. His lasting legacy, All Souls College, Oxford, continues to be a prominent institution for legal and theological scholarship.
